messages.subject: astrazeneca to work on gbm code
messages.subject_clean: astrazeneca to work on gbm code
messages.body_plain:
Hi All!

As I mentioned a while back, here at AstraZeneca we’re funding a full time software developer to work on gbm, which we use for data mining of clinical trials. What with one thing and another the project has been a little delayed from where we left it, but we’re now kicking it off.

We’ll focus on improving the maintainability, extensibility, and validation of the code; the initial phase is expected to last approximately 10 weeks starting (about) now.  We’re going to try to minimize some of the coupling between system components, increase the orthogonality of the APIs within the package, abstract data behind opaque data objects, and apply appropriate design patterns.  The API for the R GBM package will not be altered by this work.   This should make the package more maintainable and testable, and more readily parallelisable.

The development work will be partitioned into 2 week sprints; at the end of each sprint we’re going to suggest where we think we’ll be going, but we’re not yet sure what the overall roadmap will look like.  As we’ve all discussed earlier (and it’s pretty noncontentious) we’re going to start off in this sprint by refactoring how adMisc is used in the underlying C++ codebase and changing the initialization of the distribution classes.  Our target in the next sprint is (also noncontentiously) to reduce the function signatures within the C++ code by implementing an appropriate opaque data class.  We’re expecting to learn what needs doing as we go – but do please provide any input you feel is useful!

We’ll look to merge changes back into gbm-developers/gbm every two weeks.  If you want to see / comment on work in progress, look at https://github.com/scientific-computing-solutions/gbm .

pdm

messages.body_plain:
A couple months ago I posted underlying code to do the coxph caculation correctly -- the
current gbm code is not quite correct if there are any tied death times.  (Every real data
set has a few of these).  I was waiting for someone to comment on how plug it into the
framework.

> As we’ve all discussed earlier (and it’s pretty noncontentious) we’re going to start off in this sprint by
> refactoring how adMisc is used in the underlying C++ codebase and changing the initialization of the
>distribution classes.

And indeed, a key issue was that it does not fit nicely into the "adMisc" framework.  The
"y" variable is a (time, status) pair and the ancillary variable is a sort index, two
indices for the (start, stop) form of a Cox model.  Updating the sort indices for
cross-validation is another point that needs to be thought through carefully.

One reason for hearing nothing since I did that is that all are busy, another is that I
messed up the post and no one saw it.  Would someone let me know if it is the latter?
Getting the coxph code correct would be an important update of GBM -- the error in the
current result will often be small but can be substantial if there are many ties, it is
also dependent on the sort order of tied values.  Allowing (start, stop) style data would
be an important additional capability.

Terry Therneau

messages.body_plain:
I have no plans for reintroducing multinomial - we're going to have quite a bit to do with what is there at the moment, and a working TTE implementation and a fully unit-tested codebase both have approximately infinitely higher priority.

But as a side effect we should end up with pretty extensible code, and we can always reassess how we're doing a few sprints in.

pdm

grants.  Helping your team, even helping a lot, is going to be much less work than that.
Given my near zero experience with C++ the result of your team's efforts will almost
certainly be better than mine would have been.

Terry T.

messages.body_plain:
I just discovered the folds.id <http://folds.id> argument, which is very useful.
A suggestion is to allow cv.folds to be a vector or a single number; then folds.id <http://folds.id> is not
needed.  (This is what rpart does.)

It isn't a significant code change, but makes it more likely that users will find the
argument.

Terry T.
